reviews.text: This is a film that will slowly beat your heart down, begin to rebuild it, and then break it again, before finally leaving it in an achingly bittersweet place.
reviews.author: Joseph Tomastik

reviews.text: ...a very authentically felt and still-uncomfortable topic from such a saddening standpoint.
reviews.author: Christina Newland

reviews.text: I am certain that as is, The Whale (the film), struggles to say anything meaningful about people and oversells the characterizations and the relationships in a way that doesn’t feel natural.
reviews.author: Brittany Patrice Witherspoon

reviews.text: ...a project that, while certainly powerful at points, could have reached further heights if not for some very questionable calls.
reviews.author: Yasmine Kandil

reviews.text: However unsubtle with its messaging, “The Whale” is a devastating ode to the complexity of human beings, and the inner beauty one can find behind even the most destructive of feelings towards self and others.
reviews.author: Calum Cooper

reviews.text: “The Whale” works because Fraser, particularly his eyes and voice, and the rest of the cast deliver performances that imbue their two-dimensional characters with enough presence and emotion that they feel three dimensional.
reviews.author: Sarah Vincent

reviews.text: Fraser keeps Charlie’s fully formed humanity at the forefront of The Whale, despite various filmmaking decisions that could flatten his character into a saccharine pity case.
reviews.author: Soham Gadre

reviews.text: It’s Aronofsky’s most blunt and uninspired work yet— an indulgent and strident slice of misery porn that rides a wave of unearned emotion to its underwhelming conclusion.
reviews.author: Prabhjot Bains

reviews.text: If you didn’t know that The Whale was based on a play, you’d work it out pretty quickly... The immediate distance that this initially creates soon evaporates, however, in no small part thanks to Fraser’s all-in performance.
reviews.author: Damon Wise

reviews.text: If it’s as sincere as it purports to be, this is one of the worst movies of recent years, and if it’s not — which is almost preferable — then it’s a landmark exercise in trolling.
reviews.author: Farah Cheded

reviews.text: A morbidly obese man racked with self-loathing makes a desperate eleventh-hour attempt to reconnect with his estranged teenage daughter in the overstuffed but worthwhile drama, The Whale.
reviews.author: Paul Kanieski

reviews.text: Earns its place in the "most tearful films of the year" list as it moves slowly yet efficiently towards its overwhelmingly emotional ending, especially elevated by the most subtly powerful & irrefutably moving performance of Brendan Fraser's career.
reviews.author: Manuel São Bento

reviews.text: A riveting character study of one broken man that transcends compassion, love, pain/regret. A masterpiece Sadie Sink/Hong Chau should be nominated & Brendan Fraser might have turned in one of the best performances of all time
reviews.author: Zach Pope

reviews.text: I just wished that the film overall was as strong as Brendan Fraser’s acting comeback.
reviews.author: Hector A. Gonzalez

reviews.text: Charlie [is] played brilliantly by Brendan Fraser...
reviews.author: Udita Jhunjhunwala

reviews.text: It has a more or less decent preamble that is propelled by an organic performance from Brendan Fraser on his return, but its psychological marrow is locked into a basic routine of trivial conversations and a lack of substance. [Full reveiw in Spanish]
reviews.author: Yasser Medina

reviews.text: A strangely hopeful story that manages to stay on the surface even as it seems to sink into mediocrity. [Full review in Spanish]
reviews.author: Nilton Arana

reviews.text: One of the most deplorable elements of The Whale is its near celebration of defeat and resignation. The decision by Charlie to eat himself to death is treated as a meaningful act of self-sacrifice. Why would this possibly be so?
reviews.author: David Walsh

reviews.text: All the weight of the story (metaphorically and literally) is carried by its tragic protagonist — the ailing Charlie, whom Brendan Fraser portrays with such depth, nuance, and wit. Nothing in the film's text matches this commitment, and that's a problem.
reviews.author: Milana Vujkov

reviews.text: Two words - Brendan Fraser.  He was born to play Charlie and his Oscar award is extremely well deserved.
reviews.author: Allison Rose

reviews.text: Chamber settings, by their nature, let the acting echo out and Fraser’s central performance speaks volumes about his character’s history.
reviews.author: Amber Wilkinson

reviews.text: Though The Whale has captured the interest of the public, I can’t say that it’s earned. I hated this movie, but not for the reasons you may think.
reviews.author: Stacey Yvonne

reviews.text: Aronofsky’s film of this joyless play was a hit, so I guess it touched something in the moviegoing public. It had to use a bodega claw to do it because it couldn’t get off the couch, but it touched them.
reviews.author: A.S. Hamrah

reviews.text: Aronofsky uses The Whale for easy, unsightly, virtue-signaling.
reviews.author: Armond White

reviews.text: At times, it feels like they had a list of difficult themes they wanted to include, which makes for an uneven experience. But we also can't deny the power of Fraser's performance, which some would argue is superior to the film. Full review in Spanish.
reviews.author: Sebastian Zavala Kahn

reviews.text: At every moment when subtlety might afford Charlie humanity or control of his own story, Aronofsky takes the lurid path.
reviews.author: Eric Webb

reviews.text: There’s much ado about Brendan Fraser’s king-sized portrayal of a doomed 600-pound Idahoan college professor, but the stagey, often ridiculous movie he’s wedged into, alas, is thin as a rail.
reviews.author: Al Alexander

reviews.text: Even his [Brendan Fraser] unblemished commitment to the role can't redeem this intimate behind-doors drama from excessive pathos and an inordinately staged posture that makes it less genuine than it was supposed to.
reviews.author: Filipe Freitas

reviews.text: In lots of ways, The Whale is your standard Aronofsky movie. Only this time it doesn't rejoice in the main character's flaws, it uses them to tackle tough subject matters such as traumas, guilt, pain and redemption. [Full Review in Spanish]
reviews.author: Alejandro Turdó

reviews.text: Aronofsky offers an honest and authentic portrait of a man struggling to come to terms with his past and move forward, but he does so seemingly without knowing what message Charlie’s story is supposed to impart...
reviews.author: Beth McMillan

reviews.text: ... A film that never disguises its theatrical origin to the point of artificiality. [Full review in Spanish]
reviews.author: Pablo De Vita

reviews.text: It isn't a bad film, but it's not that good either, and it's worth discerning and separating, to appreciate what's fat and what's bloated. [Full review in Spanish]
reviews.author: Pablo O. Scholz

reviews.text: The Whale is indefensible, turning out to be a silly melodrama that views its protagonist with a loathing it tries to present as empathy. [Full review in Portuguese]
reviews.author: Pablo Villaça

reviews.text: It's true that the metaphor of Moby Dick's redeeming character falls into the obvious... but The Whale is much more than that: it's the last station of a life that once was full but now only awaits its end. [Full review in Spanish]
reviews.author: Ezequiel Boetti

reviews.text: The narrative oscillates constantly between exposing the clinical consequences of obesity and portraying the psychology of the protagonist. [Full review in Spanish]
reviews.author: Denise Pieniazek

reviews.text: Ultimately we come away from "The Whale" warmed by the openness of heart and spirit Fraser brings to it.
reviews.author: Rob Gonsalves

reviews.text: Aronofsky’s career-long obsession with the grotesque is alive and well here, and he skirts the edge of exploitation. But The Whale is very much a splayed-open tragedy, and a weirdly romantic one at that...
reviews.author: John Serba

reviews.text: It should come as little surprise that Aronofsky's eighth film is at its finest when it lets Fraser, Chau and Sink verbally bounce off of each other.
reviews.author: Sarah Ward

reviews.text: The Whale is set leveling the rawness of human sadness with practice sympathy and forgiveness.
reviews.author: Annie Banks

reviews.text: Incredibly moving.
reviews.author: Rosalynn Try-Hane

reviews.text: By far, his [Aronofsky] worst film. [Full review in Spanish]
reviews.author: Ruben Peralta Rigaud

reviews.text: There’s nothing consciously sinister about THE WHALE’s use of Charlie’s eating disorder (the original play was, in fact, written from experience), but Aronofsky’s adaptation is cruel, not just to Charlie’s character, but to all of them.
reviews.author: Jenny Nulf

reviews.text: The Whale is a film characterized by wall-to-wall woe and the lonesomeness and obsession felt by one doomed man. It is devastating, dark and raw, relentless in its commitment to make the audience feel something.
reviews.author: D. Patrick Rodgers

reviews.text: He doesn’t have issues with his body image – he has given up on his body altogether. He’s not unhappy because he’s fat, but fat because he’s unhappy.
reviews.author: John McDonald

reviews.text: Brendan Fraser stands out, but every member of Darren Aronofsky's tiny cast gets moments to shine, and they all prove up to the challenge. Together, they combine to tell a lovely heartbreaker of a story.
reviews.author: Mike Scott

reviews.text: Darren Aronofsky's The Whale is all of these things: a remarkable spectacle, a play adaptation, a lousy film, an Oscar-comeback vehicle for Fraser.
reviews.author: Tom Shone

reviews.text: The pathetic story of a futile repentance. [Full review in Spanish]
reviews.author: Carlos Bonfil

reviews.text: Aronofsky mistrusts the audience's capacity to understand and empathize, and feels the need to employ an irritating, tear-inducing score... [Full review in Spanish]
reviews.author: Alfonso Flores-Durón y Martínez

reviews.text: The film leaves us questioning our own conventions regarding physical appearance, the effects of homophobia, and religion as a means of escaping reality. [Full review in Spanish]
reviews.author: Gisela Savdie

reviews.text: A clunky and imbalanced chamber piece that lacks the director’s reliable visual instincts.
reviews.author: Damien Straker

reviews.text: Aronofsky builds a thorough melodrama. [Full review in Spanish]
reviews.author: Hugo Hernández Valdivia

reviews.text: Fraser is singularly heartbreaking as a man whose body stars as a mammoth monument to grief...
reviews.author: Rahul Desai

reviews.text: [Brendan Fraser is] an enchanting performer, and that’s accentuated in Darren Aronofsky’s The Whale: a film that has the actor serving as a powerful, bright light in a dark pool of despair.
reviews.author: Eric Eisenberg

reviews.text: While the film itself isn't necessarily a sum of all its incredible acting parts, The Whale is an emotionally affirming story which -- once again it seems -- feels like just what we need right now.
reviews.author: Kate Rodger

reviews.text: It might be the director’s most restrained film, but there’s beauty in its subtlety and horror in its nuance. Simply put; this is a feast of a film.
reviews.author: Ben Turner

reviews.text: The kind of film that does not work in a way that only a very fearless and bold Artist-with-a-capital-A could manage to make it not work.
reviews.author: Tim Brayton

reviews.text: It’s such a heavy-handed approach that The Whale’s extremity risks alienating the audience from the intention.
reviews.author: Wenlei Ma

reviews.text: I found this quite hammy... it feels like it's pointing and staring.
reviews.author: Stephen A. Russell

reviews.text: The Whale doesn’t shy away from questioning one’s existence and purpose of living. It isn’t an easy watch and feels deeply personal and traumatic.
reviews.author: Renuka Vyavahare

reviews.text: Best known for his turns in such schlocky adventures as George of the Jungle and The Mummy, Fraser commands undivided attention by wearing a fatsuit but never letting the fatsuit wear him.
reviews.author: Nandini Ramnath

reviews.text: The Whale is a moving, enveloping film that, while it very rarely departs from its stage origins, reaches the heights of emotional drama.
reviews.author: David Stratton

reviews.text: It’s an absolute triumph of a performance from [Brendan] Fraser, whose own humanity is what ultimately allows The Whale to not entirely sink in its surroundings.
reviews.author: Peter Gray

reviews.text: Aronofsky's The Whale isn't a conventional love story — it isn't a conventional anything — but it's about love nonetheless, both destructive and redemptive.
reviews.author: Brian Viner

reviews.text: The Whale, with its themes of redemption, family love and the boundless human capacity for caring about other people -- all fine in themselves but too melodramatic, too portentous here -- doesn’t tell us much about the psychology of obesity.
reviews.author: Markie Robson-Scott

reviews.text: There's nothing wrong with Fraser's performance, which has earned him an Oscar nomination and been ascribed that dreaded word, 'comeback'. The bigger question though is what, if anything, all of this means.
reviews.author: Paul Whitington

reviews.text: While Fraser survives with his reputation intact, this attempt at an unflinching portrait of self-destruction sees Aronofsky once again biting off more than he can chew.
reviews.author: Alan Corr

reviews.text: [A] stagey and relentlessly miserable adaptation of Samuel D Hunter’s play...
reviews.author: Andy Lea

reviews.text: …a well-crafted, traditional Hollywood stage adaptation, a success for Aronofsky and something of a triumph for the previously unfashionable Fraser, who jet-packs to prominence while poor Charlie is struggling to get in and out of his wheelchair…
reviews.author: Eddie Harrison

reviews.text: An interesting film about pity, guilt and shame. But, given Darren Aronofsky's habit of making the extremes of human experience look and feel like a horror film, I'm not sure it ever quite gets to 'empathy'.
reviews.author: Simon Miraudo

reviews.text: It's Fraser who is the outright star of this masterful film, giving such a powerful performance that it will leave even the hardest heart broken.
reviews.author: Dulcie Pearce

reviews.text: The Whale is leavened in those moments when Fraser's boyish giggle and bright-eyed wonder peek through, heartbreaking reminders of a persona that once lit up movie screens with goofy charm. But at the movie's worst, which is often, even Fraser suffers.
reviews.author: Luke Goodsell

reviews.text: The pace is so repetitive, and Charlie’s small cast of visitors keep bursting through the front door so regularly, that his sitting room comes to resemble a bus depot at peak hour.
reviews.author: Sandra Hall

reviews.text: Ultimately, it alludes to things without adding up to much of anything. Still, the performances are all excellent, and Fraser is especially compelling, bringing a sincerity to Charlie, and an openness and gentleness.
reviews.author: Deborah Ross

reviews.text: If ever a performance saved a movie, it’s Brendan Fraser in The Whale. The voyeuristic elements of the film are outshone by the humanity that radiates from its star and supporting cast, making for a flawed film that nonetheless pulls at the heartstrings.
reviews.author: Victoria Luxford

reviews.text: The film needs empathy for Charlie to have a genuine reason for being. But Aronofsky sees his characters the way certain children look at spiders. Which leg first?
reviews.author: Danny Leigh

reviews.text: Deals in the worst, most jaded conventions of bourgeois middlebrow dinner theatre from the 1950s ... Not even someone so warm as Fraser can win us over to the most jaw-droppingly daft final shot in recent cinema.
reviews.author: Donald Clarke

reviews.text: The Whale tackles a clutch of tough topics – obesity; isolation; body shaming; betrayal; forgiveness – with sensitivity and a raw honesty that can sometimes be hard to take...a pungent performance-based arthouse film made for adults.
reviews.author: Jim Schembri

reviews.text: Brendan Fraser stretches every limit in director Darren Aronofsky’s painful exploration of physical entrapment.
reviews.author: Andiee Paviour

reviews.text: A drippy, big-screen soap opera.
reviews.author: Chris Wasser

reviews.text: Aronofosky’s decision to embrace the film’s stage origins doesn’t help matters either – the stripped down aesthetic only adding to the suspicion that there’s not much more to this than the body horror spectacle of its central performance.
reviews.author: Alistair Harkness

reviews.text: A broken, bewildered, and fragile man lies at the center of a concentrated broth... where the struggle between our desire to empathize with him and Aronofsky's commitment to impeding it, boycotts the film... [Full review in Spanish]
reviews.author: Blai Morell

reviews.text: His [Brendan Fraser's] body scares, but his face and voice emote various emotions with talent, sensibility, and magnetism. This is what I like the most about The Whale. [Full review in Spanish]
reviews.author: Carlos Boyero

reviews.text: The Whale is best appreciated as a moving, stripped-back character study, with a stunning lead performance.
reviews.author: Sophie Butcher

reviews.text: [Aronofsky] centers us on the most impactful emotional journey of recent months performed by the man with the saddest, most captivating, and comprehensive stare we've seen on the big screen. [Full review in Spanish]
reviews.author: Randy Meeks

reviews.text: Brendan Fraser, cherished for his earlier roles as an endearing naïve, performs miracles in making Charlie likeable... Enduring such an awful play is a high price to pay to see some acting, though.
reviews.author: David Sexton

reviews.text: If honesty to self trumps all other values and commitments, then whatever hinders authenticity is villainized. In The Whale, the church—and its privileging of God’s revealed truth over our subjective authenticity—is thus the biggest villain.
reviews.author: Brett McCracken

reviews.text: Boasting sometimes harrowing scenes, raw emotions and confronting imagery, The Whale is a challenging watch... However, like the best art -- and to paraphrase the story’s totemic essay -- this movie will make you think about your own life.
reviews.author: James Croot

reviews.text: Aronofsky abandons the provocative, violent and very fierce gesture of his previous works to offer a fable about self-destruction that is extremely calculated and without edges. [Full review in Spanish]
reviews.author: Luis Martínez

reviews.text: Fraser manages to step over the cumbersome props to deliver one of his best performances. [Full review in Spanish]
reviews.author: Irene Crespo

reviews.text: … a tender and frequently overwhelming character drama, albeit carrying Aronofsky’s love-it-or-hate-it penchant for directness and preoccupation with metaphysics.
reviews.author: Cain Noble-Davies

reviews.text: The overall project remains compelling...
reviews.author: Robin Holabird

reviews.text: Fraser and Chau give such heartfelt performances, and Charlie's shut-in existence is so relatable in this pandemic era, that it's no surprise the movie makes many viewers weep. But its central plot mechanism feels mendacious.
reviews.author: Margot Harrison

reviews.text: This movie further bolsters director Darren Aranofsky's reputation as one of America's premier directors. Like a play, the movie takes place almost entirely in one room, confining and concentrating the drama of Charlie's loneliness and sadness.
reviews.author: Robert Roten

reviews.text: We are shown enough to surely be shocked and saddened, but we are also shown Charlie’s sweetness and desperation.
reviews.author: Steve Crum

reviews.text: The film is outstanding in telling Charlie’s story without frills, and it is firmly centered on its main character with minimal embellishments.
reviews.author: Sarah Ksiazek

reviews.text: It's an amazing film.
reviews.author: tt stern-enzi

reviews.text: ...in watching “The Whale,” a fatphobic audience might temporarily disabuse themselves of the derision and disgust they hold for the heavyset just long enough to pat themselves on the back for emotionally connecting with a cartoon for roughly two hours.
reviews.author: Dominic Griffin

reviews.text: Yes, Brendan Fraser is terrific in The Whale. So terrific that his stellar performance accentuates the picture’s overall shortcomings.
reviews.author: Robert W. Butler

reviews.text: Fraser gives a career-best performance, owning this deeply emotional story from beginning to end. So much so that the rest of The Whale is often lost in his shadow.
reviews.author: Michael Balderston

reviews.text: “The Whale’s” improbable story doesn’t ring true, yet Fraser’s performance does and for some, that may be enough.
reviews.author: Charles Koplinski

reviews.text: There's a lot to love here… I will neverwatch it agan, but I really appreciated the experience of it.
reviews.author: Jaby Koay

reviews.text: Rather than creating authentic empathy from the audience, the film is more interested in making a spectacle of Charlie’s suffering and his body.
reviews.author: Chris Feil

reviews.text: The story has obvious stage play roots with the requisite 'playing to the back row,' but the praise of Fraser's performance is legit. He provides Charlie with a sweet darkness in both the inherent positive nature of his soul and the harsh slow suicide.
reviews.author: Patrick McDonald

reviews.text: Brendan Fraser's extraordinary performance will break you heart.
reviews.author: Linda Cook

reviews.text: Director Darren Aronofsky has demonstrated a penchant for grandiose metaphysical statements in past films, such as The Fountain, Black Swan and Mother!, but he is back down to earth in his new film, The Whale.
reviews.author: Randall King

reviews.text: The Whale is a mammoth undertaking, lacking in subtlety, and compassion, that leaves the viewer gasping for air on the beach.
reviews.author: Leo Brady

reviews.text: Though all movies are subjective experiences, I would argue that Aronofsky is way too much of a provocateur to commit fully to the kind of sensitivity and empathy this material surely needed to circumvent its parade of immobile trauma.
reviews.author: Nathaniel Rogers

reviews.text: [Brendan Fraser's] acting in this film will knock your socks off. The story is as about as human as it can get with the darkness and the light vying with each other for dominance in this broken man's soul.
reviews.author: Hosea Rupprecht

reviews.text: I found something very special in here. I found a very heartfelt story about pain, loss, [and] human connection.
reviews.author: Jeremy Jahns

reviews.text: There are some fine performances by Sink as the reality of her dad’s plight pierces Ellie’s hard-bitten facade, and by Hong Chau as a private nurse whose devotion to Charlie is well beyond professional. The star turn, however, belongs to Fraser.
reviews.author: Kristian M. Lin

reviews.text: To say this movie is heavy-handed is an understatement: Aronofsky and Hunter overtly spell out the terms of Charlie’s tragic decline and assign unambiguous moral virtues to virtually all the characters onscreen.
reviews.author: Eileen G'Sell

reviews.text: In this study of a man going through addiction and loss, Fraser’s powerful performance as a compulsive eater gives this work a profound sense of pathos.
reviews.author: John Lui

reviews.text: Fraser wholeheartedly conveys Charlie with heart and humility.  He doesn't make you pity Charlie, but rather makes you connect with the emotionality and paralyzation that an emotion such a grief grabs hold on one's spirit physically and emotionally.
reviews.author: Carla Renata

reviews.text: Fraser devours every scene as Charlie. It's riveting to watch.
reviews.author: Chase Whale

reviews.text: Even in a flawed movie, it’s a beautiful subject to explore. And Aronofsky completely misses it.
reviews.author: Sean Collier

reviews.text: It’s a stunning, brave performance from Fraser, possibly his best. He depicts this bruised man as a gentle soul whose tragic flaw was caring too much in a disingenuous environment.
reviews.author: Lynn Venhaus

reviews.text: It's a heart-breaking story of regrets, grief and reconciliation that features multiple strong performances, with Fraser leading the way.
reviews.author: Micheal Compton

reviews.text: While the presentation is wrapped in a devastating and depressing narrative, at the center is a story of the enduring love of an expectant, encouraging, and inspirational father searching for meaning and redemption to pass along.
reviews.author: Chris Joyce

reviews.text: Fraser wrings more pathos out of his eyes and mouth than many actors manage with their entire bodies, delivering deep reserves of sensitivity and vulnerability.
reviews.author: Chris Knight

reviews.text: Did this film really need to get made, or was it just the least-risky project Aronofsky could shoot under lingering COVID restrictions about 20 months ago?
reviews.author: Dennis Harvey

reviews.text: (Brendan) Fraser aims for so much more in a film which lacks any hint of true empathy and understanding.
reviews.author: Michael Ward

reviews.text: If you’re going to see this film for any reason, that reason is Brendan Fraser. His performance is exceptional, though unsurprising.
reviews.author: Tim Brennan

reviews.text: Charlie’s life could’ve come off overwrought and maudlin, but Fraser brings a unique empathy to the character, who clearly doesn’t see a way out of his situation beyond no longer taking up so much space.
reviews.author: Chad Byrnes

reviews.text: Aronofsky has broached similar territory before but terrific performances by Brendan Fraser & Hong Chau reveal this to be a more layered look at the way we treat others and the empathy that often escapes us for even the most inner-flawed of people.
reviews.author: Erik Childress

reviews.text: Despite the darkness there is a light here and although it's not an easy watch at times, it will stay with you long after the film is over.
reviews.author: Paul Salfen

reviews.text: Fraser's portrayal ... is utterly transformative. Bearing witness to Fraser's genius is well worth the existential torment The Whale may inflict.
reviews.author: Candice McMillan

reviews.text: None of it is particularly easy to watch, but the gentle humanity in Fraser's demeanor will stay with you a while.
reviews.author: John Urbancich

reviews.text: Fraser ... gives an arresting performance that makes The Whale well worth seeing, despite some issues.
reviews.author: Mark Meszoros

reviews.text: The performances are good across the board (especially from Fraser who should earn every male lead acting award this year) and the film certainly delivers an emotional wallop, particularly at the end.
reviews.author: Jim Judy

reviews.text: Fraser delivers the best work of his career.
reviews.author: Richard Roeper

reviews.text: Brendan Fraser gives a transformational performance as a man filled with regret and self-loathing, but also reaching out for one last chance at love.
reviews.author: Christopher Lloyd

reviews.text: Brenden Fraser is outstanding in this role, relatable, occasionally funny, and with an endless supply of optimism that is heartbreaking.
reviews.author: Michelle Kisner

reviews.text: Because without Fraser and Chau's performances, that's all this really is: a shallow plea for kindness in a world so cynical that people have grown less accepting than they already were in hopes that God gives them a reserved seat at the apocalypse.
reviews.author: Jared Mobarak

reviews.text: 'The Whale' isn’t merely an actors’ showcase of earnest vulnerability. Aronofsky finds unique ways to make what surrounds his cast members feel just as alive with wonder and fascination.
reviews.author: Preston Barta

reviews.text: Fraser's choices are so subtly intelligent that we barely notice what amounts to his costume, so attuned are we to the way his Charlie teeters on the brink of life and death.
reviews.author: Chris Hewitt

reviews.text: Aronofsky’s claustrophobic vehicle for the acting prowess of Brendan Fraser, as well as Hong Chau, Sadie Sink and Samantha Morton. The performers deserve a less dismal vehicle... less a movie than an illustrated text,
reviews.author: Ray Pride

reviews.text: Fraser's Charlie teeters on the edge of danger and clings to the tiniest buoy of hope, one that barely floats on a sea of heartbreak.  The lead actor performance of the year.
reviews.author: Jeff Mitchell

reviews.text: Thanks to the cast, “The Whale” manages to mine some pathos despite its dispiriting story.
reviews.author: Russ Simmons

reviews.text: An emotional, heart-wrenching, deeply felt story told perfectly by a master filmmaker who knows how to get the finest performances out of his actors.
reviews.author: Alex Billington

reviews.text: His [Brendan Fraser's] performance anchors this intense and lacerating dramatic tempest. [Full review in Spanish]
reviews.author: Juanma Fernández París

reviews.text: This is an instance when one can appreciate an actor’s accomplishment while acknowledging that the vehicle to which he’s contributing isn’t worthy of his talent.
reviews.author: Frank Swietek

reviews.text: But the strength of this movie is Fraser, who delivers the best performance of the year.
reviews.author: Jonathan Sim

reviews.text: The Whale eventually disintegrates into a blunt soap opera that wildly disconnects from its noble pursuits.
reviews.author: Matt Conway

reviews.text: Brendan Fraser seems to have been preparing for this role for the last decade, pouring all his emotion into this character. It's a beautiful performance, and Sadie Sink provides great counterbalance and depth.
reviews.author: Lee McCoy

reviews.text: Brendan Fraser gives an amazing performance. The film, however, feels like an amateur play.
reviews.author: Korey Coleman

reviews.text: Brendan Fraser is fantastic, and does what he can with a thin/double-edged script/story. By far, one of Darren Aronofsky's weakest outings. [Full review in Spanish]
reviews.author: Fico Cangiano

reviews.text: Fraser makes you feel sadness and revulsion in pretty equal portions. But, the balance shifts more to sadness as we learn his reasons for his obesity.
reviews.author: Robin Clifford

reviews.text: The film is both uniquely an Aronofsky work and something quite universal, a message for those who believe their past mistakes or current self make them outcasts in their own life.
reviews.author: Steven Prokopy

reviews.text: Charlie is meant to be gawked at and pitied — and the film lets viewers do both. It is meant to jerk tears, but it feels manipulative.... Aronofsky’s heavy-handed film is crushed by the weight of its own self-importance.
reviews.author: Gary M. Kramer

reviews.text: The Whale sometimes feels more like an intrusion than a movie, invaded privacy wearing the mask of drama.
reviews.author: Robert Denerstein

reviews.text: A massive performance as a mammoth man can’t keep it from being dramatically light as a feather.
reviews.author: Todd Jorgenson

reviews.text: The bland, matted cinematography takes some zip off, but Fraser, clearly committed, carries much, and the supporting cast do their part.
reviews.author: Tom Meek

reviews.text: [Brendan Fraser's performance]  can’t quite lift this turgid chamber drama up from the depths of director Darren Aronofsky’s bloated pretensions.
reviews.author: Jay Horton

reviews.text: Whatever the intention, the effect is one of “pay the nickel, see the freak.”
reviews.author: Oscar Goff

reviews.text: The Whale is a vehicle, perhaps, but it's a vehicle for an unforgettable, maybe even classic star turn.
reviews.author: M.V. Moorhead

reviews.text: Fraser is reason enough to give The Whale a chance. The movie belongs to him, and his performance transcends its divisive provocations
reviews.author: John Paul King

reviews.text: 'The Whale' boasts great performances that show complexity in each person it examines — even if it doesn’t have time to pair down its ambiguous nature.
reviews.author: Murjani Rawls

reviews.text: Fraser and Aronofsky are forces opposed, approaching the story from disparate vantages of empathy and harsh judgment. Fraser’s movie works. Aronofsky’s isn’t so successful.
reviews.author: Siddhant Adlakha

reviews.text: What’s missing from the screenplay and in Aronofsky’s interpretation of it is an understanding of the mental unrest and overall mindset of how Charlie got to this place and why he’s still living in it.
reviews.author: Paul McGuire Grimes

reviews.text: Boring and frustrating, The Whale is not destined to have a long legacy unless Fraser truly relaunches his career. If nothing else, Fraser proves his value as a star and centerpiece of a film.
reviews.author: Alan French

reviews.text: There’s a dull but nagging falseness to the film that no amount of melodrama can fully numb. And while Aronofsky demands our empathy (more so than earning it), his film can be as mean-spirited as it is heartbreaking.
reviews.author: Keith Garlington

reviews.text: Darren Aronofsky’s “The Whale” is a film that tries to build sympathy and understanding for its dangerously obese main character. Maybe a good place to start would be to not call your film “The Whale”?
reviews.author: Rob Thomas

reviews.text: The Whale is not a cruel spectacle – it is just a dull, repetitive one.
reviews.author: Barry Hertz

reviews.text: Aronofsky has proven he can direct, so what to make of the fact that this film is so hateful and vile?
reviews.author: Odie Henderson

reviews.text: One of the best films and lead performances of the year. [Full Review in Spanish]
reviews.author: Nestor Bentancor

reviews.text: An Aronofsky movie without any of the showmanship that makes Aronofsky movies watchable. There’s not an interesting image in the entire picture.
reviews.author: Sean Burns

reviews.text: [The Whale] coasts on the back of some amazing acting, led by an all-time turn by Fraser that cuts deep into the hearts of viewers.
reviews.author: Rob Dean

reviews.text: See Brendan Fraser in a career re-defining turn as man whose body is his prison.
reviews.author: James Verniere

reviews.text: Without Fraser’s tremendous contribution and an equally praiseworthy supporting performance from Hong Chau, Aronofsky’s latest would be the filmmaker’s worst.
reviews.author: Andrew Parker

reviews.text: The Whale is messy and compromised, but finds its honesty in the emotional core of its lead performance. See it for Fraser, try and drown out the rest.
reviews.author: Adam Graham

reviews.text: A murky-looking, claustrophobic exercise in emotionalism at its most trite and ostentatiously maudlin.
reviews.author: Ann Hornaday

reviews.text: While The Whale makes for distressing viewing at times, it is balanced out by compassionate storytelling and well-rounded characters, making this one of Aronofsky’s most relatable films.
reviews.author: Alex Bentley

reviews.text: This is all about Brendan Fraser’s career-defining performance. There are plot points that don’t entirely work to benefit the experience, but some of the dialogue is riveting. Every moment Charlie is on screen will have viewers locked in.
reviews.author: Austin Burke

reviews.text: A searing, moving experience.
reviews.author: Soren Andersen

reviews.text: The Whale is a heartbreaking film with an astounding performance by Brenden Fraser—he is the reason to see it.
reviews.author: Julian Lytle

reviews.text: In every scene, every moment, practically, Fraser strives for and often succeeds in finding something more than cheap pathos.
reviews.author: Michael Phillips

reviews.text: Aronofsky and Hunter shape a largely riveting study of regret and release, rewarding patience with sharp character studies and an authentic understanding of shame.
reviews.author: Brian Orndorf

reviews.text: The best performance in the film actually comes from Samantha Morton, who in one scene burns the house down expressing every emotional stage of a marriage and its broken aftermath.
reviews.author: Laura Clifford

reviews.text: Despite what redemption there ultimately is, The Whale is a feel-bad movie. But in a movie marketplace saturated with homogeneity, at least it inspires you to feel something.
reviews.author: Jim Slotek

reviews.text: For as good and convincing as Fraser is, and I’m genuinely thrilled for his “comeback,” “The Whale” stumbles in confronting its main characters' morality and his search for something greater than himself.
reviews.author: Nate Adams

reviews.text: Most of the conflicts in The Whale are overcooked nonsense, contrived for dramatic impact but divorced from any recognizable reality.
reviews.author: Scott Tobias

reviews.text: A divisive whale of a tale that features Brendan Frasers most devastating on screen work to date.
reviews.author: Dustin Chase

reviews.text: It features one great and a couple of really good performances. But it is not a great movie. I’m not even sure it’s much of a good one.
reviews.author: Bill Goodykoontz

reviews.text: It’s the director’s tendency to underline every point, every symbolic connection, and make them unmistakable for the viewer that leaves The Whale feeling like a lofty yet tedious exercise.
reviews.author: Brian Eggert

reviews.text: The comeback story for Fraser is heartwarming, but his performance here is like watching someone run into a burning building. There’s a deep riskiness to it that puts the entire film in jeopardy every five minutes, but Fraser never hits a false beat.
reviews.author: Cory Woodroof

reviews.text: [Brendan] Fraser is devastatingly good ... but filmmaker Darren Aronofsky has done the broken father-daughter relationship better, [and Sadie] Sink brings no nuance to her role.
reviews.author: Kiko Martinez

reviews.text: The Whale is a thematically muddled film that prioritizes melodrama over character but is nevertheless elevated by a committed cast.
reviews.author: Brandon Zachary

reviews.text: The devastating ending emotionally manipulates you into believing the production is more cathartic than uncomfortable to behold. Ultimately what redeems The Whale in the end, are Fraser and Chau’s resolute portrayals in a very maudlin movie.
reviews.author: Eric Marchen

reviews.text: What appeared to be a well-meaning film has ended up as part of a long line of art about fat people that ends up trafficking in the same tropes around representing fat people. The Whale is a movie that doesn’t know when it should have flinched.
reviews.author: Elamin Abdelmahmoud

reviews.text: "I shouldn’t ask because I know the answer, but why are filmmakers [...] so blind to the fact that it is the prejudices reinforced by lazy narratives like these that do us the most harm?"
reviews.author: Cate Young

reviews.text: A man facing imminent death finds small joys and reason to laugh and looks forward to his release. Charlie's an example of apparent weakness and carelessness who is wide awake and strong.  Extraordinary stuff. Haunting, demanding and oh-so human.
reviews.author: Anne Brodie

reviews.text: "The Whale" will be a challenge for some impatient viewers but rewarding for those up for an intellectual conversation about end-of-life matters that we all will inevitably experience.
reviews.author: Jonathan W. Hickman

reviews.text: For better or worse, the "Black Swan" and "Requiem for a Dream" auteur cannot help himself with his edgy preferences. A humane story like "The Whale," even with its own grimness, doesn’t need Aronofsky’s heavy darkness to be effective.
reviews.author: Don Shanahan

reviews.text: One wishes the film was as great as Fraser's fearless raw emotional performance, but we can forgive many of its deficiencies... Charlie's quest for transcendence echoes every queer person's struggle for dignity and respect.
reviews.author: Brian Bromberger

reviews.text: Darren Aronofsky's adaptation of screenwriter Samuel D. Hunter's play is empathetic & soulful. What's most memorable is Brendan Fraser's performance, demonstrating how his impressive talent was perhaps wasted in "Mummy" and "George of the Jungle" movies.
reviews.author: Susan Granger

reviews.text: The powerful performances of both Sadie Sink and Brendan Fraser will likely garner Oscar nods. Whether you consider the ending happy or sad depends entirely on how you expected it to end. Regardless, The Whale leaves you feeling emotionally wrung out.
reviews.author: MontiLee Stormer

reviews.text: The script is absolute drivel, a patently phony work that betrays its roots as a stage play at every turn.
reviews.author: Jason Bailey

reviews.text: The Whale is a vivid portrait of our inability to escape our own sadness when it becomes all-consuming and of those who are willing to hold our hands through it all.
reviews.author: Josie Meléndez

reviews.text: If you get it, you get it… It’s not for everyone and some will not comprehend the why, but I’m going to tell you "The Whale" is a MASTERPIECE. Easy Oscar nod for Frasier for this standout performance! The last act I was sobbing to the point of breaking.
reviews.author: Samuel Leggett Jr.

reviews.text: “The Whale” doesn’t make a lunge for your emotions. It earns them.
reviews.author: Mick LaSalle

reviews.text: Fraser was by a mile the best part of this film. He brings gravitas and a great deal of thoughtfulness to it... The problem I had with the film was everything else.
reviews.author: Lael Loewenstein

reviews.text: Stagy and sometimes overwrought, but it really is a heartbreaking, emotional journey.
reviews.author: Claudia Puig

reviews.text: This film is well crafted and well-acted, though questions about its purpose - why is this difficult movie about a very difficult man even made - unanswered.
reviews.author: J. Don Birnam

reviews.text: Wants us so desperately for us to believe in simple human goodness, to look beyond appearances and even actions and see something beautiful, and yet it treats Fraser's character with such disgust that it is disturbing for all the wrong reasons.
reviews.author: Mattie Lucas

reviews.text: It can be relentless in its depiction of gluttony as a means of self-flagellation... There is no happy ending for Charlie, and in one moment where he can finally show others he’s a man who deserves dignity, perhaps that is enough.
reviews.author: Alan Zilberman

reviews.text: Finds humanity and honesty in each one of its troubled characters. ... The film evokes Aronofsky’s The Wrestler and is one of his most empathetic works.
reviews.author: Eric Ortiz García

reviews.text: While some will resist the film's sentimental approach, others will be profoundly moved.
reviews.author: Rich Cline

reviews.text: Two hours of contrived miserablism posturing as an exercise in radical empathy.
reviews.author: Isaac Feldberg

reviews.text: I am not opposed to body horror, but the genre is best suited to vulgar ends. The Whale is presenting itself as something noble and, ultimately, uplifting, but it just can’t make that sale.
reviews.author: David Sims

reviews.text: The movie might largely be remembered for being somber, an emotion that stays at the forefront of the narrative, but it’s optimism that buoys its ending.
reviews.author: Candice Frederick

reviews.text: Fraser deserves praise for his buried-under-makeup performance, but that’s not enough to keep the movie afloat.
reviews.author: Brian Lowry

reviews.text: Whatever 'The Whale's many imperfections, Brendan Fraser's relentless display of craft and courage is a must see.
reviews.author: Rex Reed

reviews.text: The Whale just needs one house, six performers and Brendan Fraser's blue eyes to prove once again that theatricality in cinema can result into truly wonderful experiences.
reviews.author: Víctor López G.

reviews.text: Beneath the pain, the anguish, the prosthetics, Fraser does something miraculous. Anchoring Charlie’s trauma in his own, the once A-list star taps his publicly-recorded anguish and ostracism and turns it into something truly transcendent.
reviews.author: Matt Oakes

reviews.text: The Whale feels like an end-of-the-world yarn that makes you want to smile and embrace those close to you with all their imperfections and shortcomings.
reviews.author: Shikhar Verma

reviews.text: Aronofsky has the subtlety of a sledgehammer, yet I found this to be his most earnest and heartfelt film yet. Also, let's not forget the top-tier performances of Fraser and Chau.
reviews.author: EJ Moreno

reviews.text: The Whale aims for empathetic humanism. Instead, it exposes a callous voyeurism.
reviews.author: Natalia Keogan

reviews.text: Like Darren Aronofsky's other movies, this dark drama doesn't shy away from the realities of its main character's situation, but what lingers are its deep wells of compassion.
reviews.author: Jeffrey M. Anderson

reviews.text: The director leaves viewers little room not to be reminded of what makeup artists can do in their craft.
reviews.author: Kent Turner

reviews.text: This chamber piece amounts to a variation of torture porn for highbrows, with a fat suit rather than a meat cleaver as the bringer of cinematic shock.
reviews.author: Kyle Smith

reviews.text: Brendan Fraser gives a great performance in this complex and touching story of redemption.
reviews.author: Kevin Carr

reviews.text: For every sunbeam of humanity Fraser lets shine through this soul, the film summons a half-dozen dark clouds to try and dampen it.
reviews.author: David Fear

reviews.text: The Whale tries to awkwardly straddle the ciphers of Aronofsky’s allegorical obsessions with the sins of some very too-real flesh, and it comes up wanting.
reviews.author: Jason Adams

reviews.text: “The Whale" could be considered Oscar bait on a fat-suit hook, cast by a manipulative angler with tons of cinematic chum in the water if not for a deeply human performance by Brendan Fraser, making a serious swim toward the Oscars in a welcome comeback.
reviews.author: Jason Fraley

reviews.text: Like Charlie, The Whale itself has mobility issues. It goes nowhere. It threatens to buckle under its own weight, as a surging, string-laden score attempts to convey poignancy in a script and performances that come to us already slick with tears.
reviews.author: Rich Juzwiak

reviews.text: [The Whale] gawks at the grotesquerie of its central figure beneath the guise of sentimentality, but it also offers sharp exchanges between its characters that ring with bracing honesty.
reviews.author: Christy Lemire

reviews.text: Brendan Fraser is on the march to Oscar. That's how astonishing he is as a morbidly obese recluse in this deeply moving character study. Accusations that wearing a fatsuit diminishes his tour de force performances are nonsense. This is essential viewing.
reviews.author: Peter Travers

reviews.text: Aronofsky has a tender regard for the problems endured by the overweight: negotiating the complexities of bathrooms, struggling to force wheelchairs through too-narrow doorways, dropping a set of keys on the floor...
reviews.author: Kurt Loder

reviews.text: If only this precious defense of the chroniclers weren't blasted out of the arena by the strutting and mewling of crowing pontificators.
reviews.author: Walter Chaw

reviews.text: A movie that strives to wrest something raw and truthful from a story that’s all bald contrivances, technological as well as melodramatic.
reviews.author: Justin Chang

reviews.text: “The Whale” may not be as honest as Charlie demands, but Fraser is, and that is the film’s saving grace.
reviews.author: Katie Walsh

reviews.text: The Whale has impactful performances that get viewers to react on a visceral level. People will think about what makes them uncomfortable in this story, which takes an emotional journey into the type of life that some people think should be hidden.
reviews.author: Carla Hay

reviews.text: What makes it a must-see is Fraser’s daring, difficult, deeply moving performance as an infinitely kind and regretful man at the end of his rapidly fraying rope
reviews.author: Tim Appelo

reviews.text: This is a film that stays with you and changes you. It is heavy, indeed.
reviews.author: Mark Kennedy

reviews.text: The script is clunky, doling out background information about the characters at regular intervals, while the parallels between “Moby Dick” and Charlie’s life would make any real English teacher ask for a second draft.
reviews.author: Steve Erickson

reviews.text: One might approach it to get a look at a transformed Brendan Fraser, but by the end, few will be looking outward at all, instead looking inward at their own failures of kindness, perhaps with a renewed dedication to openness.
reviews.author: Dan Scully

reviews.text: Fraser reminds audiences that he's just as much of an acting powerhouse as ever, with his costars only managing to heighten his performance, though the experience stumbles with some clunky blocking and dialogue.
reviews.author: Patrick Cavanaugh

reviews.text: Brendan Fraser delivers a searingly sad, soulful performance in Director Darren Aronofsky’s gripping drama about a 600 pound man whose vulnerability is so transparent, yet so moving.
reviews.author: Linda and Al Lerner

reviews.text: The Whale ends with a scene that brings out the best of Sink and Fraser, where the characters reach their emotional fill, breaking all their inhibitions.
reviews.author: Abhishek Sharma

reviews.text: It’s unfortunate that I find the deliberate ways in which stage play adaptations retain certain qualities to feel like a hindrance... With that in mind, Fraser certainly earns the plaudits given thus far, as does the rest of this cast,
reviews.author: Aaron Neuwirth

reviews.text: The Whale...offers few moments of hope and no truly happy resolutions (but) you stick with this guy through thick and thicker, simultaneously repulsed and intrigued thanks to a fierce performance of a lifetime by Brendan Fraser.
reviews.author: Bill Newcott

reviews.text: It is a work that positions itself as about meaning and connection, of finding the beauty in the minutiae of life (like an essay written by a child that offers comfort), but it has no interest in the humans it features.
reviews.author: Juan Barquin

reviews.text: Screenwriter Samuel D. Hunter ... doesn't quite seem to know which argument of the many possibilities here he actually wants to make, let alone develop.
reviews.author: Mark Dujsik

reviews.text: Unfortunately for a film claiming that the body is nothing but a container for the soul, the performance ends up being more surface, less vital spirit.
reviews.author: Murtada Elfadl

reviews.text: An unflinching, heartbreaking and haunting emotional journey. Brendan Fraser gives a raw, brave performance. It's, by far, the best performance of his career.
reviews.author: Avi Offer

reviews.text: Fraser touches your emotions. Whatever your opinions of the choices Charlies has made, he is not a bad man.
reviews.author: Bob Bloom

reviews.text: “The Whale,” like some of Aronofsky’s other projects, is swamped by its grand and vague ambitions. It’s overwrought and also strangely insubstantial.
reviews.author: A.O. Scott

reviews.text: This is very much an arthouse stunt movie, but it's the kind of arthouse stunt that makes me appreciate arthouse stunts.
reviews.author: Vincent Mancini

reviews.text: 'The Whale' is its own parody, a rejection of all the lessons society should've learned over the last decade about what happens when you give every reactionary forum avatar a megaphone and call it connection.
reviews.author: Jon Negroni

reviews.text: “The Whale” makes waves in two ways: for Brendan Fraser’s astounding and incredibly compassionate portrayal of an obese man seeking redemption, and as an empathy test in a supremely cynical social-media landscape.
reviews.author: Brian Truitt

reviews.text: The six-minute standing ovation Fraser received in Venice wasn’t long enough.
reviews.author: Michael Nordine

reviews.text: This is not a subtle film. Superior work from the cast, Fraser in particular, proves enough to make that lack of subtlety overlook-able.
reviews.author: Mike McGranaghan

reviews.text: The cynic in me believes this movie may have been constructed primarily for end-of-the-year plaudits because there doesn’t seem to be another compelling reason for it to exist.
reviews.author: James Berardinelli

reviews.text: A constant battle between Brendan Fraser's sincere performance and a complete caricature of a prosthetic contraption. Fraser ultimately wins but the prosthetic contraption puts up a good fight for two hours.
reviews.author: Fred Topel

reviews.text: Fraser carries the entire project on his shoulders, and you see the fire in his eyes in every frame.
reviews.author: Rendy Jones

reviews.text: The Whale is in dire need of sincerity, expecting to draw empathy when it can't even find it in its own lead character.
reviews.author: Jeff Nelson

reviews.text: It's quite the experiment in misery porn; it’s hard to watch yet impossible to turn away from.
reviews.author: Mike Massie

reviews.text: With "The Whale," Aronofsky and Charlie practically gorge, and their ravenous appetites feed our own hunger: a hunger for melodrama, empathy and truth.
reviews.author: Cameron Meier

reviews.text: A struggle to watch at times simply because of how it will make viewers reflect on their own lives, this movie packs an emotional punch that will not soon be forgotten.
reviews.author: Tessa Smith

reviews.text: “The Whale” is laughably earnest, larded with melodrama, and designed to shut down the long-standing association of human bulk with high spirits.
reviews.author: Anthony Lane

reviews.text: The whole experience of watching The Whale was excruciating and it felt like it would never end. No thanks.
reviews.author: Rachel Wagner

reviews.text: Brendan Fraser gives a transcendent, once-in-a-lifetime performance, with everyone else at the top of their craft. No one finds beauty in misery like Darren Aronofsky, and The Whale is his latest stroke of mastery
reviews.author: Robert Kojder

reviews.text: [A] peculiar and often deeply unpleasant movie...
reviews.author: Dana Stevens

reviews.text: The Whale won’t be for everyone, but it should, at the end of the day, get Brendan Fraser the award recognition he rightfully deserves.
reviews.author: Rachel Leishman

reviews.text: I was not prepared for the level of craftsmanship and empathy that is present in The Whale. Regardless of everything else, Aronofsky directs his film with masterful strokes, composing an intricate harmony of image and sound.
reviews.author: Maria Lattila

reviews.text: What redeems this film, to the point of needing to be seen, is witnessing a spectacular Brendan Fraser, who does not let the character swallow him. [Full review in Spanish]
reviews.author: Alejandro Alemán

reviews.text: Brendan Fraser delivers a superb and convincing performance even as director Darren Aronofsky favors no-frills scatology.  [Full review in Spanish]
reviews.author: Fabiola Santiago

reviews.text: Without condescension, Aronofsky throws us into the void of the irreparable.  [Full review in Spanish]
reviews.author: Erick Estrada

reviews.text: It is simply unfathomable to even consider Fraser not receiving a Best Actor nomination for this performance... truly astonishing.
reviews.author: Dallas King

reviews.text: While the stagey, melodramatic 'The Whale' is far from a perfect film, it provides the right vehicle for Fraser to showcase his staggeringly impressive dramatic chops.
reviews.author: Doug Jamieson

reviews.text: Fraser pushes past all the aesthetic barriers to deliver a compelling, moving, and nuanced performance. [Full Review in Spanish]
reviews.author: Ricardo Gallegos

reviews.text: As the motley crew comes and goes, they each reveal their great psychic wound in a dramatic monologue, boiling things down to some version of hurt people hurt people each time. .
reviews.author: Tricia Gilbride

reviews.text: Darren Aronofsky's The Whale broke me. A heartbreaking and numbing cinematic journey through redemption and self-reflection. Brendan Fraser is nothing short of transcendent in this devastating and career-defining performance.
reviews.author: David Gonzalez

reviews.text: As the end credits roll on Aronofsky’s most humanistic and hopeful film, the power of Fraser’s searingly honest, career-best performance lingers. Its beauty may just leave you feeling a little more hopeful for humanity too.
reviews.author: Luke Channell

reviews.text: As such, it is a bit of a claustrophobic chamber piece. That could work, but the greater sin is the fatphobia stamped in every single scene.
reviews.author: Christopher Llewellyn Reed

reviews.text: It might lose its way at times and doesn’t seem to be able to distinguish between genuine care for its moribund protagonist and exploitative gazing, but you feel its heart is in the right place, anchored by an incredible performance from Brendan Fraser.
reviews.author: Daryl MacDonald

reviews.text: A sharp script is delivered with slow brutality by Darren Aronofsky who gets to the heart of what it means to be Charlie. The Whale isn’t just a great film -- it’s an important one, too.
reviews.author: Ryan Leston

reviews.text: "The Whale" sits on the edge of being a meaningful portrait of a suffering outcast. It just never quite reaches what it sets out to be.
reviews.author: Karen M. Peterson

reviews.text: Fraser’s lead performance absolutely ripped my heart right out of my chest to the point where I found it difficult to breathe. He’s that good.
reviews.author: Louisa Moore

reviews.text: It’s a heart-breaking and harrowing film, and one you should be cautious to watch if you’ve struggled with eating disorders, but it has such a noble heart despite its vile undertones that it somehow ends up being one of Aronofsky’s most uplifting films.
reviews.author: Jennifer Heaton

reviews.text: The Whale is a high-concentrate dose of Darren Aronofksy’s specialty, be it a balm or poison: harrowing majesty, headlined by Brendan Fraser in one of the most devastating performances of the 21st century.
reviews.author: Cameron Frew

reviews.text: Fraser's performance relies on a gentle, even beguiling belief in dignity for all.
reviews.author: Josh Larsen

reviews.text: The real sin is that Aronofsky only has eyes for Charlie’s flesh and completely fails to notice that Charlie, like all the characters in this movie, is paper thin.
reviews.author: Charlotte O'Sullivan

reviews.text: You’ll gaze dumbfounded at the screen for 1h 57m. Pulled into an emotional black hole that offers no easy exit. That’s an incredible, mind-numbing feat.
reviews.author: Dwight Brown

reviews.text: The Whale lives and dies on the strength of Brendan Fraser's lead performance, and there are few actors who deserve a career resurgence as much as he does. It's just a shame that there isn't more here beyond its function as a star-remaking vehicle.
reviews.author: Audrey Fox

reviews.text: Led by Brendan Fraser's commanding performance, The Whale is a devastating and intimate tale of broken souls in search for redemption. [Full Review in Spanish]
reviews.author: Rene Sanchez

reviews.text: Paired with Sadie Sink’s fierce performance as his callous and jaded daughter, the two make for the perfect pair to bring Aronofsky’s tragic tale to life, and their pas de deux performances make The Whale one of TIFF’s best.
reviews.author: Lauren Coates

reviews.text: At times, it feels like you’re watching a stage play, but Fraser’s performance is one for the ages.
reviews.author: Randy Myers

reviews.text: Mean-spirited while claiming to be empathetic, it consists almost entirely of people shouting mean things at each other in a way that feels manipulative, and it has almost no handle on most of its characters.
reviews.author: Stephen Silver

reviews.text: The Whale borders on body horror, but the real horror is the simple lack of compassion shown to a character in such clear emotional pain.
reviews.author: Sarah Marrs

reviews.text: “The Whale” is trapped in its own limited perspective. It cannot see beyond itself and feels stagnant, like Charlie's house. It is a woefully superficial rendering of a would-be tragic figure without the care and thought to stop and consider why, or how.
reviews.author: Andrew Kendall

reviews.text: There’s no question that Fraser has given one of his finest performances.
reviews.author: Max Covill

reviews.text: The Whale unfolds as a series of heavy-handed metaphors in search of realistic dramatic shading. They don’t find it...
reviews.author: Adam Nayman

reviews.text: There are so many aspects of The Whale that parallel Fraser’s own life, and how he was able to pull off some of these emotionally heartbreaking scenes is nothing short of remarkable.
reviews.author: Scott Menzel

reviews.text: The Whale offers a transformative experience thanks to the heart Fraser summons from deep within the belly of his prosthetics.
reviews.author: Pat Mullen

reviews.text: It is a testament to the genuineness of Fraser and Chau that the film manages to scrape by as it does, flaws and all.
reviews.author: Tomas Trussow

reviews.text: Aronofsky, artisan of lost souls, finds compassion in the oddest of situations.
reviews.author: Peter Howell

reviews.text: As a story, The Whale is compelling. As a film, The Whale is a tad shakier.
reviews.author: Alissa Wilkinson

reviews.text: Packing the most powerful performance of the year in Brendan Fraser’s comeback, everything about The Whale screams of the 90s – for better and for worse.
reviews.author: Hannah Lodge

reviews.text: Fraser, so good, takes what could be a joke, a flat tragedy, or even a lecture about weight and imbues it with gorgeous humanity.
reviews.author: Johnny Oleksinski

reviews.text: Powered by Fraser's performance, the film has moments of gentle vulnerability & contemplation in its exploration of guilt, redemption, grief & trauma.
reviews.author: Mae Abdulbaki

reviews.text: The movie’s problem, or rather the frustration I had while watching it, is the way the performances and overall aesthetics often feel in opposition to each other.
reviews.author: Jesse Nussman

reviews.text: There’s precious little truth in Charlie’s Job-like buffet of tribulations, trapping him in a film as stifling as his airless home.
reviews.author: Charles Bramesco

reviews.text: Despite the best efforts of the stars involved, The Whale is a specular failure of empathy, that prattles on about truth for almost two hours… but offers little more than shadows on a cave wall.
reviews.author: Sarah Kurchak

reviews.text: Even if it is often despite the script's more frilly flourishes, it offers a substantial emotional payload.
reviews.author: Piers Marchant

reviews.text: The Whale [doesn't] fully commit to its miserabilism – instead, that gives way to a pretty banal denouement of tearful redemption that should earn the film undue awards consideration.
reviews.author: Sam C. Mac

reviews.text: The last 10 minutes of The Whale are sublime. Everything else is just dead weight.
reviews.author: Gayle Sequeira

reviews.text: The Whale is pathetic, yet it’s not because of our protagonist’s circumstances or the tumult he is put through: [Aronofsky] loses sight of the wonderful gift he’s been given by his lead.
reviews.author: Nick Johnston

reviews.text: While the body padding transforming Fraser is a stunt, his performance certainly isn’t.
reviews.author: Ty Burr

reviews.text: Darren Aronofsky's testament to empathy and redemption shatters you, before putting you back together. Brendan Fraser gives the performance of a lifetime. Once The Whale grabs you, it will not let go.
reviews.author: Joey Magidson

reviews.text: The spectre of death hangs over every frame of “The Whale,” and yet Fraser manages to bring optimism to a character not long for this world.
reviews.author: Richard Crouse

reviews.text: Darren Aronofsky’s The Whale is an act of hate disguised as tough love.
reviews.author: Katie Rife

reviews.text: [Fraser] brings a sensitivity and dignity to the film where others may have played the audience for pity or comedy.
reviews.author: Rachel Ho

reviews.text: With The Whale, Darren Aronofsky brings a hollow sense of dignity to his schematic brand of cinematic misery porn.
reviews.author: Mark Hanson

reviews.text: It often feels clumsy and maddeningly inconsistent, stranding Fraser in a melodrama undeserving of his lovely, unshowy performance.
reviews.author: Leah Greenblatt

reviews.text: This devastating portrait of one man’s unyielding grief and his need to seek redemption through those closest to him, is handled with a great deal of empathy from Aronofsky, and will break your heart in two.
reviews.author: Alysha Prasad

reviews.text: The hype is real, Brendan Fraser is extraordinary.
reviews.author: Chris Bumbray

reviews.text: The Brenaissance is here.
reviews.author: Nicholas Barber

reviews.text: The elaborate full-body makeover of The Whale is no less real than anything else in this fatally overwrought melodrama of compulsion and atonement.
reviews.author: A.A. Dowd

reviews.text: It's a redeeming film about salvation, that has great performances from the talented cast and a superb one from Fraser.
reviews.author: Dennis Schwartz

reviews.text: The Whale captivates from start to finish. For a film that has one set and stars an actor who’s barely mobile, that’s a remarkable achievement however you slice it.
reviews.author: Zhuo-Ning Su

reviews.text: The Whale is meant to be a poignant consideration of guilt, sexuality, religion, remorse. We really only know that, though, because the movie shouts it at us.
reviews.author: Richard Lawson

reviews.text: [The Whale] is stagy and mawkish. Watching it, you feel grossly manipulated but the approach is undeniably effective.
reviews.author: Geoffrey Macnab

reviews.text: Fraser is certainly a showstopper here, and his level of emotional prowess of the kind but broken Charlie is so exceptional it often forgives a stagey theatricality Aronofsky can’t quite avoid.
reviews.author: Nicholas Bell

reviews.text: Alongside The Wrestler, The Whale is Aronofsky at his most compassionate. It’s a gargantuan invitation to empathy and understanding.
reviews.author: John Bleasdale

reviews.text: With The Whale, Aronofsky and Fraser have taken substantive risks, in the name of an insistent empathy. I think, and my tear ducts agree, that those risks paid off.
reviews.author: Glenn Kenny

reviews.text: Once everything finally collides in The Whale, something shattering and beautiful and honest emerges.
reviews.author: Bilge Ebiri

reviews.text: [Brendan Fraser's] performance is strangely beautiful, one of those rare roles that seems to draw on years, if not decades, of a performer’s personal misfortunes and harness them into something profound.
reviews.author: Rory O'Connor

reviews.text: Body horror takes a new form in Darren Aronofsky’s The Whale, which chronicles the long, slow suicide of a morbidly obese man with pitiless candour but an abundance of empathy.
reviews.author: Raphael Abraham

reviews.text: Fraser is courageous and fully committed in his first major leading feature film role for around a decade.
reviews.author: Wendy Ide

reviews.text: The Whale builds slowly but surely towards that mad coup de grâce, which will either leave you cold or sweep you heavenward: for me, it was a quintessential Aronofsky flourish; as loopily sublime...
reviews.author: Robbie Collin

reviews.text: Quibbles and conversation starters aside, The Whale is Aronofsky's kindest work to date, a film that asks its audience to practice acceptance, understanding, empathy, and forgiveness.
reviews.author: Jane Crowther

reviews.text: A worthy comeback for King Brendan.
reviews.author: Hannah Strong

reviews.text: Without Brendan Fraser’s innate charm and ability to project gentle sadness through the slightest flicker of his huge blue eyes, “The Whale” wouldn’t have that much else going for it.
reviews.author: Leila Latif

reviews.text: Hunter’s script and the intimacy of the actors’ work keep the melancholy drama grounded and credible.
reviews.author: David Rooney

reviews.text: Most of “The Whale” simply isn’t as good as Brendan Fraser’s performance. For what he brings off, though, it deserves to be seen.
reviews.author: Owen Gleiberman

reviews.text: The writing clunks; the narrative is contrived and unconvincing and the whole film has a strange pass-agg body language, as if it is handling its own painful subject matter with kid gloves and asking us to do the same.
reviews.author: Peter Bradshaw

reviews.text: Sometimes an actor can help minimize a director’s shortcomings, and that’s what Fraser does here.
reviews.author: Stephanie Zacharek

reviews.text: This is a transcendent, triumphant film. Without doubt, the Oscar race has begun and Aronofsky and Fraser are at the head of the queue.
reviews.author: James Mottram

reviews.text: Brendan Fraser tackles this role with such grace and compassion for the character and, by extension, the real people out there who will see themselves in him.
reviews.author: Lex Briscuso

reviews.text: It is inorganic, gimmicky, manipulative, and its lessons are simplistic. As a character, Charlie remains mostly a body. He has a kindness to him, but this role is mostly to react to the wants and needs of others.
reviews.author: Brian Formo

reviews.text: What "The Whale" boasts in abundance — in this riveting study of a deeply broken man, suffocated by nine years of self-immolation — is a rare and deep compassion, elevated by Brendan Fraser’s transformative turn.
reviews.author: Jack King

reviews.text: The fact that Fraser is so good in the role and that Aronofsky is so skilled at shaping the performance combine to make “The Whale” a uniquely powerful film experience.
reviews.author: Tom O'Brien

reviews.text: Most of the fatalism comes from a heavy-handed style that sees this closed world as a closed circuit, a place for figurative characters to come and express what they Represent. And then to come back the next day and do it again.
reviews.author: Ben Croll

reviews.text: The Whale wouldn’t be as effective if it wasn’t for the incredible lead performance given by Brendan Fraser...and I don’t think anyone could have played Charlie the way Fraser did.
reviews.author: Robert Ruggio

reviews.text: Brendan Fraser is easily the best part of Darren Aronofsky's otherwise derivative The Whale.
reviews.author: Marshall Shaffer

synopsis: A reclusive English teacher suffering from severe obesity attempts to reconnect with his estranged teenage daughter for one last chance at redemption.
